title: Format Specifiers and Formatted Input and Output
learningObjectives: Explain the central rules behind format specifiers and formatted input and output in C.
Identify the relevant types, declarations, operators or library facilities.
Trace a worked example and explain its result.
Recognize common mistakes, portability concerns and unsafe assumptions.
Apply the concept in a small program and test normal and boundary cases.

understand.concept: Formatted I/O functions use a format string to convert between textual representations and C values. printf-family functions receive values, while scanf-family functions generally receive pointers to destination objects. The conversion specification must match the argument type and required pointer type; mismatches can cause undefined behaviour.
understand.whyItMatters: Input and output are where program data crosses a textual boundary. Correct format strings, return-value checks and input validation prevent corrupted values and misleading output.
understand.analogy: Think of a type as a contract that describes what kind of value an object can hold and which operations make sense for it.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only an introduction; C types also determine representation, conversions, alignment and constraints.

explain.narrative:
Formatted I/O functions use a format string to convert between textual representations and C values. printf-family functions receive values, while scanf-family functions generally receive pointers to destination objects. The conversion specification must match the argument type and required pointer type; mismatches can cause undefined behaviour.

Input and output are where program data crosses a textual boundary. Correct format strings, return-value checks and input validation prevent corrupted values and misleading output.

When reviewing code, identify the declared types first, then trace conversions and the exact expression being evaluated. Compile with warnings enabled and test boundary values. Do not rely on assumptions about another compiler or machine.

examples.title: Core example
examples.code: int count = 7;\nsize_t length = 12;\nprintf("count=%d length=%zu\\n", count, length);
examples.explanation: %d formats an int and %zu formats a size_t. Match each conversion with the exact promoted argument type.

examples.title: A second case
examples.explanation: scanf needs the address of the destination object and returns the number of successfully assigned input items. Production input handling should also consider trailing characters and line boundaries.

practise.guidedTask: Print an int, unsigned int, size_t, double and string with correct conversion specifications. Then read an integer and check the return value before using it.
practise.independentTask: Build a robust record-input routine that reads a full line, validates its length and converts numeric fields with an appropriate checked conversion function.
hints: printf formats values; scanf usually stores into objects through pointers.
Check scanf's return value before reading the destination variable.
Never use untrusted text as a printf format string.
Prefer line-based input and explicit parsing for robust user input.
